nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Year-round warm sunshine drives growth in the rainforest canopy, clearings and mangroves.

nodes.name: Tropical rain
nodes.desc: Heavy rainfall keeps the lowland rainforest of the peninsula lush and the soils and swamps wet.

nodes.name: Tidal sea water
nodes.desc: Twice-daily tides flood the coastal mangroves and bring in salt water and sediment.

nodes.name: Forest soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and dead animals are broken down and the nutrients return to the soil for plants to use.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Eupatorium (Siam weed)
nodes.desc: Leafy shrub that Wikipedia says Javan rhinos feed on. Its feeding grounds in the park shrank from 158 ha to 20 ha by 2013.

nodes.name: Arenga palm
nodes.desc: A fast-growing palm that shades the forest floor and reduces the food available to rhinos, so authorities work to remove it.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Figs are among the coastal and forest plants of the park and are a food source for fruit-eating birds and mammals.

nodes.name: Rainforest fruit trees
nodes.desc: Fruiting trees such as Aglaia, whose fruits are recorded as eaten by macaques, fruit bats and civets.

nodes.name: Mangroves
nodes.desc: Mangroves such as Rhizophora and Sonneratia line the coast of the park in salt-tolerant stands.

nodes.name: Grasses
nodes.desc: Grasses of open ground and clearings that feed grazing deer and cattle.

nodes.name: Javan rhinoceros
nodes.desc: Critically endangered browser of shoots, twigs and fallen fruit. Ujung Kulon holds its only known wild population, about 82 animals per Wikipedia.

nodes.name: Banteng
nodes.desc: Wild cattle that compete with rhinos for feeding grounds in the park. Recorded prey of leopards and dholes.

nodes.name: Javan rusa
nodes.desc: A deer of forest edges and open ground and the most recorded large mammal in the area.

nodes.name: Indian muntjac
nodes.desc: Small forest deer that eats foliage and fallen fruit; recorded as prey of leopards and dholes.

nodes.name: Long-tailed macaque
nodes.desc: A common monkey that eats fruit and is recorded eating the fruits of Aglaia and Antidesma.

nodes.name: Lesser short-nosed fruit bat
nodes.desc: A fruit bat recorded eating Allophylus fruit; spreads seeds as it feeds.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: Omnivore that roots in the soil and eats fruit. Recorded prey of leopards, dholes and pythons.

nodes.name: Asian palm civet
nodes.desc: Fruit-eating forest civet recorded eating Aglaia fruit; leopards are recorded to prey on it.

nodes.name: Reticulated python
nodes.desc: Huge constrictor recorded taking monkeys, wild boar, mouse-deer and water monitors.

nodes.name: Asian water monitor
nodes.desc: Opportunistic large lizard that often scavenges carrion and also takes monkeys and small deer; recorded as prey of reticulated pythons.

nodes.name: Javan leopard
nodes.desc: Top predator of the peninsula since the Javan tiger disappeared in the mid-1960s. Recorded eating banteng, dhole, muntjac, civets and boar.

nodes.name: Dhole
nodes.desc: Pack-hunting wild dog that mainly takes medium and large hoofed animals; recorded taking banteng, muntjac and wild boar, and the Javan rusa is a named prey.
